## Methods

Materials
ITO-coated glasses, cesium iodide (CsI, 99.998%), lead bromide (PbBr2, 99.99%), and bathocuproine (BCP, 99%) were purchased from Advanced Election Technology Co., Ltd. Lead iodide (PbI2, 99.999%) was purchased from Alfa Aesar. Formamidinium iodide (FAI, 99.99%) and methylammonium iodide (MAI, 99.99%) were purchased from Greatcell Solar Limited (Australia). Poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA, 99%), lead sulfocyanide (Pb(SCN)2, 99.5%), PEDOT:PSS (Clevios VPAI 4083), and C60 (99%) were purchased from Xi’an Polymer Light Technology Corp. [2-(9H-Carbazol-9-yl)ethyl] phosphonic acid (2-PACz) and ethylenediamine dihydroiodide (EDAI2, >99%) were purchased from TCI Shanghai. Strontium iodide (SrI2, 99.99%), tin iodide (SnI2, 99.99%), tin(II) fluoride (SnF2, 99%), ammonium thiocyanate (NH4SCN, 99.99%), isopropanol (IPA, 99.8%), chlorobenzene (CB, 99.8%), N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.8%) and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.8%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. Copper (Cu, 99.99%) and silver (Ag, 99.99%) were purchased from ZhongNuo Advanced Material Beijing Technology Co., Ltd. Unless stated otherwise, all materials were used as received without further purification.

Precursor preparation
Wide-bandgap FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I1-xBrx)3 perovskite precursor preparation. The FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I1-xBrx)3 (x=0.15, 0.2, 0.4) perovskite precursor solution (1.5 M) was prepared by dissolving 1.2 mmol FAI, 0.3 mmol CsI, 1.5(1–1.5x) mmol PbI2 and 2.25x mmol PbBr2 in 1 ml mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO with a volume ratio of 7:3. Then 9.69 mg Pb(SCN)2 was added into the solution as additives. The perovskite precursor solution was thoroughly mixed and aged for 2 h before using. Then the solutions were filtered through polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) syringe filters (0.45 μm) before use.

Small-bandgap FA0.95Cs0.05PbI3 perovskite precursor preparation. 1.5 M FA0.95Cs0.05PbI3 perovskite precursor was prepared by dissolving 1.35 mmol FAI, 1.65 mmol PbI2, and 0.15 mmol CsI in 1 ml mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO with a volume ratio of 4:1. The precursor was stirred for over 2 h and then filtered by using a 0.45 μm PTFE syringe filter before use.

Narrow-bandgap Sn-Pb perovskite precursor preparation. 46.8 mg CsI, 414.9 mg PbI2, 14.1 mg SnF2, 85.8 mg MAI, 185.7 mg FAI, 335.3 mg SnI2, and 2.7 mg NH4SCN were dissolved in 1 mL mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO with a volume ratio of 3:1. The precursor was stirred for 10 h at 50°C. The solution was shaken to be dissolved in the glove box.

Device fabrication
Fabrication of small-area PSCs. The indium-doped tin oxide (ITO) glass substrates were ultrasonically cleaned by deionized water, IPA, and acetone sequentially, and dried in an oven. The substrates were then subjected to UV-ozone treatment for 15 min and transferred to a glove box for device preparation.

Fabrication of hole transport layer and WBG FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I1-xBrx)3 (1.65 eV, 1.68 eV, and 1.78 eV) and small-bandgap FA0.95Cs0.05PbI3 perovskite films. For the HTL layer, 50 μL of the PTAA/CB solution (5 mg mL−1) was spin-coated on UV-ozone plasma-treated ITO glass substrate at 6000 rpm for 30 s, followed by annealing at 100°C for 10 min. After cooling down to room temperature, 50 μL of the 2-PACz/DMF solution (10 mg mL−1) was spin-coated onto the ITO/PTAA substrate at 3000 rpm for 30 s and annealed at 100°C for 5 min to improve its wettability67. The perovskite precursors were blade-coated at a blade speed of 5 mm s−1 with a gap of 100 μm, and 10 μL of perovskite ink was used for each coating. During blade-coating, an N2 flow below 20 psi was applied to facilitate the solvent evaporation and perovskite crystallization. Then, the as-prepared perovskite films were transferred onto a hotplate and annealed at 105°C, verified by an infrared thermometer (Supplementary Fig. 43). After 10 min, the perovskite film at 105°C was immediately soaked into SrI2/IPA solution (0.2 mg mL−1) for 5 s, which was cooled to 5°C in advance as the quenching liquid. The quenching speed was estimated to be 20°C s−1. After that, the perovskite film was tempered at 105°C to complete the quenching treatment. Finally, 20 nm C60, 7 nm BCP, and 80 nm Ag were sequentially deposited on the perovskite films via thermal evaporation (Suzhou Fangsheng FS-450) to complete the devices.

Fabrication of hole transport layer and NBG Cs0.1FA0.6MA0.3Sn0.5Pb0.5I3 perovskite films. The PEDOT:PSS aqueous solution was spun onto the substrates at 4000 rpm for 30 s, then annealed at 150°C for 20 min. The Sn-Pb alloying perovskite films were deposited via a two-step spin-coating process, namely, 1000 rpm for 10 s and then 4000 rpm for 40 s, respectively. 200 μL of CB was poured on the spinning substrate after reaching 4000 rpm for 25 s. The substrates were immediately annealed at 120°C for 10 min. The perovskite films were prepared in a glove box filled with an inert nitrogen atmosphere (O2 <0.01 ppm, H2O <0.01 ppm) to carefully prevent Sn2+ oxidation. Finally, 30 nm C60, 5 nm BCP, and 150 nm Cu electrode were sequentially deposited via thermal evaporation. For the completed PSCs, they were either protected in an inert atmosphere or with appropriate encapsulation during testing and characterization.

Fabrication of PSMs. The fabrication process of the PSMs was similar to that of small-area devices except for the dosage of the precursor and the laser scribing patterning process. The schematic of fabrication procedures, including all deposition and scribing steps are as follows (Supplementary Fig. 33). With an aperture area of 10.4 cm2, the module’s layout was designed as a monolithic interconnection of four subcells, each with a 0.67 cm width. Firstly, the ITO-coated glass was etched by a laser scribing process with a 532 nm wavelength laser, yielding a P1 line width of 27 μm. The deposition of all functional layers followed the procedures used for small-area cells, but with adjusted solution quantities, namely, 500 µL for HTL deposition and 20 µL for perovskite layer blade-coating. P2 scribing was performed after the deposition of the perovskite/C60/BCP layers to scribe a line width of 120 μm. After Ag deposition, P3 was performed to scribe a line width of 59 μm, achieving the geometrical fill factor (GFF) of up to 95% for the modules, exhibiting an active area of 10.13 cm2.

Characterization
Steady-state and temperature-dependent photoluminescence (PL) spectra were obtained by FLS1000 (Edinburgh Instruments Ltd.), equipped with a Xe lamp, a liquid nitrogen cryostat (Oxford Instruments, Optis-tat DN-V), and a photomultiplier tube (PMT) detector. The excitation wavelength was 470 nm. PL mapping measurements were conducted using Morpho PG2000-PRO. The morphological features of the samples were characterized using a field emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi-SU8010) that executed at 2 kV. The atomic force microscopy (AFM) measurements were performed on a Scanning Probe Microscope (Bruker Dimension Fastscan, Bruker, Germany). The XRD patterns were characterized on an X-ray powder diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation of 1.5418 Å (Rigaku, Japan). Time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectroscopy (ToF-SIMS) measurements were carried out using a ToF-SIMS 5, ION-TOF GmbH. In situ PL measurements under light stress were performed using a mercury lamp light source (OLYMPUS, U-HGLGPS), which provided 130 W output in the 460–490 nm range. GIWAXS images were collected using a Xeuss 2.0 spectrometer (Xenocs company) with MetalJet-D2 (Excillum) as the X-ray source and Pilatus 3R 1M (Dectris) as the detector. Glancing incident angle X-ray diffraction (GIXRD) was performed on a D8-discover 25 diffractometer (Bruker). Valence band (VB) measurements were performed via UPS, employing a bias of 5 V and Au as a reference. Illumination intensity-dependent photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) measurements were conducted using the LuminQY system (Ideaoptics). The femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy was conducted by equipping a regeneratively amplified Ti:Sapphire laser source (Coherent Legend, 800 nm, 150 fs, 5 μJ mpulse−1, and 1 kHz repetition rate) and Helios (Ultrafast Systems LLC) spectrometers. A 75% portion of the 800 nm output pulse was frequency-doubled in a BaBO (BBO) crystal, which could generate 400 nm pump light. Meanwhile, the remaining portion of the output was concentrated into a sapphire window to produce a white light continuum (320–780 nm) probe light. The 400 nm pump beam was generated as part of the 800 nm output pulse from the amplifier, and its power was adjusted by a range of neutral-density filters. The pump beam was focused at the sample with a beam waist of 360 μm; the power intensity was fixed at 14 μJ cm−2 in this experiment. With the aid of the mechanical chopper, the pump repetition frequency was synchronized to 500 Hz. The probe and reference beams could be split from the white-light continuum and sent into a fiber optics-coupled multichannel spectrometer by complementary metal oxide-semiconductor sensors with a frequency of 1 kHz. The J-V characteristics and the steady photocurrent under maximum power output bias (1.05 V) of PSCs/PSMs were measured in ambient air (25°C ± 5°C and 40% ± 10% relative humidity) using a Keithley 2400 source-meter under simulated AM 1.5G one sun illumination (100 mW cm−2) generated by a solar simulator (the Oriel Sol3A Class AAA) based on Xenon lamps. The light intensity was calibrated by a silicon reference cell equipped with a SCHOTT visible color KG3 glass filter (Newport 91150V). All the devices were tested using non-reflective shadow masks with an aperture area of 0.04 cm2 for the small-area devices and 10.4 cm2 for the large-area PSMs, respectively. The J-V curves were measured from 1.4 V to -0.1 V or from -0.1 V to 1.4 V for the small-area devices, and from 5.5 to -0.1 V or from -0.1 to 5.5 V for the large-area PSMs with a scan rate of 0.1 V s−1. For the space charge limited current (SCLC) test, the J–V characteristics were measured using a CHI Instruments CHI660 electrochemical workstation (ChenHua, China) in a shield box with a structure of ITO/SnO2/perovskite/C60/BCP/Cu. External quantum efficiency (EQE) was measured with the solar quantum efficiency measurement system (SCS10, Zolix Instruments Co., Ltd., China) at wavelength regions from 300 to 850 nm. The optical photo of scribing for subcell separation in modules was conducted by an optical microscope (Olympus BX53MRF-S).

Light stability test. The devices used for the operational stability test were encapsulated by cover glass with edges sealed by butyl tape. The long-term MPP tracking of the encapsulated devices was carried out on the Multi-Channels Solar Cells Stability Test System (Wuhan 91PVK Solar Technology Co. Ltd, China) in ambient air with a relative humidity of 50% ± 5%, following the protocol (ISOS-L-1). The digital source meter (Keithley 2400) was used to record the current density-voltage (J–V) data under AM 1.5G one sun illumination (100 mW cm2).

Thermal stability test. The devices were placed on a heating stage at 65°C ± 5°C in a N2 glove box with encapsulation, following the ISOS-D-2I protocol. The thermal stability assessments were carried out by repeating the J-V characterizations upon heating the devices for different durations.

Statistical analysis
All statistical analysis was performed with Origin 2021. For TA data normalization, the maximum values of the dynamic TA decay lifetime were normalized to 1. To investigate the PCE statistical distribution of small-area PSCs, the histograms of 20 solar cells were used to generate the device performance statistics (Fig. 5g) and calculate the average PCEs with standard deviation (Table 1). To investigate the PCE statistical distribution of large-area PSMs, the histograms of 16 solar modules were used to generate the device performance statistics (Fig. 6b) and calculate the average PCEs with standard deviation (Table 2).

resilience of perovskite films. These synergistic effects collectively improve device efficiency
and operational lifespan of PSCs, particularly under light and thermal stress.
Regarding the driving force for secondary crystallization, we note that the temperature
difference alone is insufficient to explain the observed recrystallization. The film quality
improvement arises from a combination of thermodynamic, kinetic, and chemical driving
forces. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1, pre-annealing of wet-film at 105 °C drives the initial
rapid crystallization and forms a metastable, defect-rich perovskite framework with high free
energy, providing a thermodynamic impetus for structural evolution. The subsequent quenching
into ~5°C SrI /IPA introduces transient thermal stress, partial surface solubilization by IPA, and
2
a steep chemical potential gradient of Sr2+ and I- across the film-solution interface. These factors
collectively promote Sr²⁺ incorporation, halide compensation and passivation, and local mass
transport. Finally, the re-annealing (also called “tempering”) step allows sustained solid-state
diffusion, enabling deeper Sr2+ penetration and favorable secondary crystallization for improved
film quality, as confirmed by larger grain size (Supplementary Fig. 4), enhanced crystallinity and
relieved tensile stress (Fig. 3), and reduced defect density (Fig. 5e and 5f).
In summary, the SSQ treatment leverages the inherent instability of the initial film, kinetically
driven quenching, and chemical potential guidance from the solution, consolidated by thermal
annealing, to achieve gradient doping, surface-to-bulk defect passivation, and comprehensive
secondary crystallization (Supplementary Fig. 1). While the SSQ platform is versatile
(demonstrated with EDAI ), SrI is particularly advantageous due to its multi-faceted

stabilization effects at the atomic level, directly addressing key instability pathways in
perovskites. To clarify these issues, relevant discussion has been added in the revised manuscript.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment and for emphasizing the
importance of providing clear and convincing experimental evidence to support the proposed
SSQ mechanism. In response, we have conducted additional experiments and substantially
strengthened the mechanistic validation in our revised manuscript. The detailed responses are as
follows:
i) Film temperature before quenching
We appreciated the reviewer’s careful observation regarding the precise temperature of the
perovskite film prior to quenching. The temperature of 105 °C was not an estimated value but
the set temperature of the hotplate used during pre-annealing. To rigorously verify that the film
itself reached this temperature, we directly measured the temperature of a large-area perovskite
film on the hotplate using an infrared thermometer under identical annealing conditions. As
shown in Supplementary Fig. 42, the surface temperature of the film uniformly reached 105 °C,
demonstrating excellent agreement with the hotplate set-point. This confirmed the accuracy and
reliability of our reported experimental conditions. Relevant discussion has been added in the
revised manuscript.
As can be seen on Page 33, “Then, the as-prepared perovskite films were transferred onto a
hotplate and annealed at 105 °C, verified by an infrared thermometer (Supplementary Fig. 42).”
ii) Sr2+ doping process during quenching and tempering
We fully agree with the reviewer that elucidating the Sr2+ doping process is crucial to
understand the SSQ mechanism. To directly probe this, we performed time-resolved
photoluminescence (PL) measurements from both the front (quenched side) and rear (glass
side) of the films after quenching, followed by tempering annealing for varying durations (0-120
s). At 0 s (quenching only, without tempering), the front-side PL intensity increased, while
the rear-side PL showed negligible change, indicating that Sr2+ incorporation and defect
passivation were initially confined to the surface region. As the tempering time increased,
the rear-side PL intensity gradually rose and eventually saturated after 100 s, following the front-
side saturation (~80 s). This distinct temporal evolution provides direct experimental evidence
that Sr2+ doping and associated defect passivation proceed progressively from the surface into
the bulk of the film during the tempering step, driven by solid-state ion diffusion. This process
is schematically illustrated in the Supplementary Fig. 13 and discussed in the main text of revised
manuscript.
As can be seen on Page 11, “To unravel the kinetics of Sr2+ incorporation, we monitored the
evolution of passivation by measuring the PL intensity from both the front and rear sides of the
film after quenching and during subsequent tempering (Supplementary Fig. 13). The front-side
PL intensity increased immediately after quenching, and saturated after 80 s, indicating rapid
surface passivation. In contrast, the rear-side PL intensity remained low without tempering and
increased gradually upon annealing, saturating after ~100 s. This delay demonstrated that Sr2+
doping occurred via a time-dependent, solid-state diffusion process during tempering,
enabling the passivating species to propagate from the surface into the bulk, thereby
achieving comprehensive film improvement.”
iii) Clarification on the “coffee-ring” effect and its relevance
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which allows us to clarify a key aspect of
our innovation. There seems to be a misunderstanding that we would like to address respectfully.
The coffee-ring effect we discuss is not associated with our blade-coated perovskite film
itself, but rather with the conventional spin-coating post-treatment process that our SSQ
technique aims to replace. In traditional post-treatments, spin-coating often causes non-uniform
solute distribution due to Marangoni convention and differential solvent evaporation, resulting
in well-known “coffee-ring” phenomenon. While this may be acceptable for small-area films, it
leads to serious inhomogeneity in large-area modules. In contrast, our SSQ technique completely
circumvents this issue by immersing the entire film into the quenching solution, thereby
eliminating the convective flows-induced coffee-ring effect and non-uniformities. This ensures
a homogeneous and isotropic supply of SrI across the entire film surface, guaranteeing uniform
2
surface reconstruction and defect passivation, showing a decisive advantage for scalable
fabrication. This is precisely the rationale behind developing the SSQ approach, and the uniform
PL intensity distribution across large-area blade-coated perovskite films, as shown in Fig. 1d-i,
directly validated its effectiveness. We have revised the manuscript to make this distinction and
the associated advantage of our SSQ method explicitly.
As can be seen on Page 9, “This limitation originates from Marangoni convection during the
conventional spin-coated post-treatment, where differential solvent evaporation rates on the wet-
film surface creates radial temperature and concentration gradients, leading to solute
accumulation at the droplet edges ("coffee-ring" effect). Such inhomogeneous deposition hinders
uniform surface reconstruction and induces localized chemical heterogeneity. This effect
becomes more pronounced as the film area increases, causing discontinuities in carrier transport
channels and large interfacial charge transport barriers. In contrast, our SSQ technique
completely circumvents this issue by immersing the entire film into the quenching solution,
thereby eliminating the convective flows-induced coffee-ring effect and non-uniformities. This
ensures a homogeneous and isotropic supply of SrI across the entire film surface, guaranteeing
2
uniform surface morphology and comprehensive defect passivation, showing a decisive
advantage for scalability.”

perovskite photovoltaics. By integrating rapid cold/thermal shock-driven surface reconstruction
and gradient Sr2+ doping conveniently into one-step, the solution soaking quenching (SSQ)
technique simultaneously realized atomic-level lattice stabilization, surface morphological
optimization and compositional homogenization. As a result, the SSQ-derived devices yielded

perovskite solar modules into real-world realms from portable electronics to intelligent
photovoltaic glazing (27.12% efficiency) are interesting and meaningful. In my opinion, the
demonstrated novel processing technique particularly useful for the large-area perovskite solar
modules should be beneficial for perovskite researchers in both academic and industrial sectors.

Comment #5: It is observed that there is hysteresis disparity between spin-coated (SC) and
solution-soaking quenching (SSQ)-treated modules (e.g., PCE gap upon reverse and forward
scan, Table 2). The authors are suggested to provide the mechanistic insights about this
phenomenon.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful observation and constructive tips.
Undesirable ion migration has been widely observed and reported in perovskites and has been
regarded as one of the main origins responsible for anomalous J–V hysteresis and inferior
stability in the perovskite solar cells. (Nat. Commun., 2016, 7, 10334; Nat. Mater., 2015, 14,
193–198). We attributed the reduced hysteresis in SSQ-treated modules primarily to the
formation of improved quality perovskite films with enhanced crystallinity and less defects, as
well as suppressed halide phase separation owing to the Sr2+-assisted halide homogenization and
stabilization. Relevant discussion has been added in the revised manuscript.
As can be seen on Page 26, “The reduced hysteresis in SSQ-treated modules can be attributed
to the improved quality of perovskite films with enhanced crystallinity and less defects, as well
as favorable halide homogenization and stabilization, which is beneficial to suppress ion
migration under operational bias.”

Response to Reviewers’ Comments
REVIEWER #2
The authors have made substantial revisions in response to the reviewers' comments, which have
further improved the overall quality of the manuscript. However, there are several issues that
still require clarification or revision.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewers for the thorough evaluation and constructive
suggestions, which have prompted us to perform additional experiments and refine our
interpretations. Accordingly, we have conducted new characterizations to directly probe the
iodine compensation mechanism and have revised the manuscript to more accurately describe
the structural evolution induced by the SSQ treatment. Our detailed responses are as follows.
Comment #1: Firstly, the assertion that "the rapid quenching promoted secondary
recrystallization and halide redistribution throughout the bulk, relieving residual stress and
stabilizing the crystal lattice" is not substantiated by the present study's experimental findings,
which do not provide sufficient evidence to support the proposed iodine compensation
mechanism. In particular, no direct characterization is presented to demonstrate how the SrI /IPA
2
solution quenching treatment compensates for iodine vacancies. The provision of additional
experimental data and analyses is encouraged to provide substantiation for this claim.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s emphasis on providing direct experimental evidence for
the proposed iodine compensation mechanism. In response, we performed X-ray photoelectron
spectroscopy (XPS) measurements on both control and SrI /IPA SSQ-treated perovskite films to
2
analyze the surface halide compositions. The XPS results revealed an obvious increase in the
surface I/Pb atomic ratio from 2.07 for the control film to 2.26 for the SSQ-treated film, which
was much closer to the ideal stoichiometric ratio (~2.4). Even when accounting for potential
partial substitution of Pb2+ by the incorporated Sr2+ (Sr/Pb= ~0.5%), the adjusted I/(Pb+Sr) ratio
still reaches ~2.24, which remains substantially higher than that of the control counterpart. These
XPS data provide direct evidence that the SrI /IPA quenching medium supplies additional halide
2
ions (I-) that could be incorporated into the perovskite lattice, thus effectively compensating for
iodine vacancies and improving the intrinsic stability of resultant perovskite films (J. Am. Chem.
Soc., 2020, 3989-3996; ACS Nano, 2025, 42826-42834). We have added these new data and
corresponding discussion in the revised manuscript.

Comment #2: Moreover, the evidence supporting the occurrence of "secondary recrystallization"
remains insufficient. It is a well-established fact that recrystallization in perovskite thin films is
generally associated with pronounced grain boundary migration and a significant increase in
grain size. However, these characteristics were not observed in the present study. Instead, the
experimental results appear to be more consistent with surface reconstruction or localized
structural reorganization of the perovskite films. In view of these findings, it is recommended
that the authors reconsider the application of the term "secondary recrystallization" in this
context, or alternatively, furnish more substantial evidence to substantiate its occurrence.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion, which has helped us to describe
the SSQ mechanism more accurately. We agree with the reviewer that the term “secondary
recrystallization” may imply extensive grain boundary migration and dramatic grain growth with
enlarged size, which were not the predominant features observed in our films. Instead, the
structural improvements induced by SSQ are more accurately described as “surface
reconstruction” coupled with lattice reorganization and stress relief. In light of this, we have
revised the relevant descriptions throughout the manuscript to replace “secondary
recrystallization” with more precise terms such as “surface reconstruction” or “localized
structural reorganization”.
